Every Thursday, my neighbor puts a chair at the end of her driveway.

She doesn’t sit in it. She sets it facing the street, wipes the seat with a cloth, and goes back inside. An hour later, she retrieves it.

For months I watched this ritual from my kitchen window. I invented explanations: a memorial, a protest, an experiment in whether strangers would steal a chair.

One afternoon I finally asked.

“It’s for the bus driver,” she said. “He gets here early and takes his break across the street. His back bothers him.”

I looked across the street. There was a bus stop, a narrow strip of shade, and a man eating an orange in the chair.

“Does he know you put it out for him?”

“Oh, yes,” she said. “He used to bring his own, but it broke.”

The following Thursday it rained. From my window, I saw the chair under a large umbrella, its handle wedged through the slats. The bus driver sat beneath it, peeling his orange carefully, keeping the curls of rind out of the puddles.
